title: Hybrid Quantum Neural Networks: Theory, Implementations, and Applications
authors: Léo Monbroussou, Maniraman Periyasamy, Viacheslav Kuzmin, Pavel Sekatski, Viktoria Patapovich, Asel Sagingalieva, Alexey Melnikov
abstract: Artificial intelligence has been transformed by deep neural networks, yet the search for new learning architectures continues. Quantum machine learning offers one such direction, and hybrid quantum neural networks, which combine classical neural-network components with quantum information processing units, have emerged as a practical framework for near-term quantum technologies. However, the rapid development of the field across diverse architectures, benchmarks and hardware assumptions makes it difficult to assess the utility of various proposals, identify where genuine advantages may arise, and determine how practitioners can use these models. While recent benchmarks caution that such gains have not yet been demonstrated at scale, theoretical work has identified tasks on which quantum models hold provable advantages, and hybrid approaches have delivered promising results on practical problems using deliberately compact quantum components and substantially fewer trainable parameters. Here, we review hybrid quantum neural networks for the machine-learning and quantum-machine-learning communities. We summarize their main theoretical and methodological foundations, survey some of the most promising architectures developed so far, and examine their implementation challenges and reported performance. By consolidating these perspectives, this review provides a structured view of the state of the field and helps identify promising paths for future research and application-driven development.
summary: This review surveys Hybrid Quantum Neural Networks, a framework combining classical and quantum computing units to advance machine learning. It details how HQNNs are designed to utilize the exponential power of quantum circuits while remaining practical under current noisy hardware constraints. The paper aims to provide a roadmap for future research by structuring the state-of-the-art in this rapidly evolving field.
main_problem: The field seeks new learning architectures beyond deep neural networks, leading to the investigation of Hybrid Quantum Neural Networks (HQNNs). These are designed to leverage quantum computation where it offers a principled advantage while delegating bulk processing to classical components.
main_result: The review provides a structured view of HQNNs, summarizing their theoretical foundations and practical applications by combining classical feature extraction with quantum subroutines for enhanced learning capabilities.
method: The approach involves designing hybrid architectures that combine classical neural network layers (for high-dimensional feature processing) with variational quantum circuits (VQC) acting on exponentially large Hilbert spaces.
model_or_system: HQNNs are the core model, combining classical components with quantum information processing units. The underlying physical platform is constrained by the Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) regime.
key_observables: Model performance scaling laws, quantum advantage demonstration in specific tasks, and spectral structure representation.
important_parameters: Quantum Volume, physical qubit count, computational budget, and the degree of noise/error inherent to NISQ devices.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that genuine quantum advantages exist for certain structured or quantum-native problems, even if current empirical evidence is mixed.

paper_structure: The paper reviews the theoretical foundations, surveys promising architectures, and examines implementation challenges of HQNNs for both machine learning and quantum machine learning communities.
why_interesting: It directly addresses the practical intersection of advanced ML theory with near-term quantum hardware limitations (NISQ), which is crucial for developing algorithms applicable to open quantum systems simulations or measurement analysis.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Architecture example of a hybrid quantum neural network. A classical computer handles data pre- and post-processing, parallel co-processing, and parameter optimization, while a quantum circuit (parameterized by trainable angles) applies a unitary transformation in an exponentially large Hilbert space that, together with data encoding and measurement, realizes a nonlinear input–output map which can be hard to reproduce classically.

FIG. 2: Exponential growth trends in quantum hardware and Quantum Machine Learning (QML) research. (a) Quantum Volume of Quantinuum’s trapped-ion processors (H1 and H2 series) [1, 2]. (b) Physical qubit count of IBM’s superconducting processors; filled symbols are realized devices, open symbols are published roadmap targets [3–5]. (c) Number of papers published per year containing the phrase “Quantum Machine Learning” in the title or abstract, as indexed by OpenAlex [6] (covering arXiv preprints, journal articles, and conference proceedings). The orange bar denotes the most recent year (partial data from early July 2026).

FIG. 3: The trade-off between the two main data-encoding strategies, illustrated on 𝑛= 4 qubits. (a) Angle encoding: parameters are trivially encoded into angles of a circuit, populating all 2𝑛basis states with amplitudes that are nonlinear (trigonometric) products of the data.
